title: What is a "distributed monolith" (services that deploy/fail/scale together via shared libraries, shared DBs, synchronous chains), and how do you avoid it?
shortTitle: What is a "distributed monolith," and how do you avoid it?

s1_definition.profdef: A distributed monolith is a system split into multiple services that nonetheless cannot deploy, fail, or scale independently, so it has the operational complexity of microservices but none of their benefits. The telltale symptoms are services forced to deploy together because they share a code library whose change requires redeploying all of them, services sharing one database so a schema change breaks several services at once, and long synchronous call chains where one service calls another calls another, so a single slow or failed service cascades into failures everywhere. You avoid it by giving each service its own database, sharing contracts rather than code, replacing synchronous chains with asynchronous events where possible, and adding resilience patterns so services are genuinely decoupled in deployment, failure, and scaling.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India split one giant department into several smaller departments to be modern, but then chained them so tightly that nothing improved. The loan department and the account department share one filing cabinet (shared database), so the moment one reorganizes the files, the other breaks. They all use the same rulebook binder (shared library), so updating one rule means re-printing and re-issuing the binder to every department on the same day. And to approve one loan, the loan clerk must phone the account clerk, who must phone the fraud clerk, who must phone the credit clerk, all waiting on the line (synchronous chain), so if any one clerk is on a tea break the whole approval freezes. The bank now has many departments with all the coordination headaches of separation but still fails and deploys as one — the worst of both worlds.
s1_definition.oneliner: A distributed monolith is microservices that still deploy, fail, and scale together through shared databases, shared code, and synchronous call chains, giving you all the complexity of distribution with none of the independence — avoid it by isolating data, sharing contracts not code, and decoupling with async events.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A distributed monolith is a system split into multiple services that nonetheless cannot deploy, fail, or scale independently, so it has the operational complexity of microservices but none of their benefits. The telltale symptoms are services forced to deploy together because they share a code library whose change requires redeploying all of them, services sharing one database so a schema change breaks several services at once, and long synchronous call chains where one service calls another calls another, so a single slow or failed service cascades into failures everywhere. You avoid it by giving each service its own database, sharing contracts rather than code, replacing synchronous chains with asynchronous events where possible, and adding resilience patterns so services are genuinely decoupled in deployment, failure, and scaling.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India split one giant department into several smaller departments to be modern, but then chained them so tightly that nothing improved. The loan department and the account department share one filing cabinet (shared database), so the moment one reorganizes the files, the other breaks. They all use the same rulebook binder (shared library), so updating one rule means re-printing and re-issuing the binder to every department on the same day. And to approve one loan, the loan clerk must phone the account clerk, who must phone the fraud clerk, who must phone the credit clerk, all waiting on the line (synchronous chain), so if any one clerk is on a tea break the whole approval freezes. The bank now has many departments with all the coordination headaches of separation but still fails and deploys as one — the worst of both worlds.

**One line to remember:** A distributed monolith is microservices that still deploy, fail, and scale together through shared databases, shared code, and synchronous call chains, giving you all the complexity of distribution with none of the independence — avoid it by isolating data, sharing contracts not code, and decoupling with async events.

sections.s2_technical:
The whole point of microservices is independence: each service deploys on its own schedule, fails without taking others down, and scales to its own load. A distributed monolith has split the code across the network but kept the coupling, so it loses that independence while paying the full tax of being distributed — network latency, partial failures, distributed debugging, and operational overhead. Recognizing the symptoms is the key skill.

The first symptom is shared databases. When several services read and write the same database tables, they are coupled through the schema. A change to a column forces coordinated changes and simultaneous redeploys across every service touching that table, and one service's heavy query can starve the others. They cannot evolve their data independently, which is the heart of service independence. The fix is database-per-service: each service owns its data exclusively, and others access it only through that service's API or through events, never by reaching into its tables.

The second symptom is shared libraries that carry business logic or domain models. If services depend on a common library that contains shared domain code, then changing that library forces rebuilding and redeploying every service that uses it, so they deploy together. The fix is to share contracts, not code: publish API schemas (OpenAPI), event schemas (Avro or Protobuf), and thin client stubs, but keep business logic inside each service. Some shared utility code is acceptable (logging config, common DTO serialization), but shared domain logic is the trap. A small example of the right boundary is sharing an event schema `TransferCompleted` that both producer and consumer agree on, while each service implements its own handling logic.

The third symptom is long synchronous call chains. When service A must call B, which calls C, which calls D, all synchronously and all within one user request, the request's latency is the sum of all hops and its availability is the product of all their availabilities, so reliability drops fast as the chain grows. Worse, if D is slow, A's threads block waiting, exhausting A's thread pool and cascading the failure backward. The fix is twofold: prefer asynchronous event-driven communication where the business flow allows, so A publishes an event and moves on rather than blocking on a chain, and where synchronous calls are unavoidable, add resilience — timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, and fallbacks — so one slow dependency cannot drag down its callers.

A fourth, subtler symptom is temporal coupling in deployment: if you must deploy services in a specific order or all at once for the system to work, they are not independent. This usually traces back to the first three causes plus breaking API changes. The fix includes backward-compatible API evolution (never break a contract; add new versions and deprecate old ones) so a consumer and provider can deploy in any order.

How you avoid a distributed monolith overall: start from clear service boundaries aligned to business capabilities (bounded contexts) so services genuinely own distinct responsibilities and data; give each service its own database; share contracts and schemas, not domain code; favor asynchronous events over synchronous chains; evolve APIs in a backward-compatible way; and add resilience patterns to any remaining synchronous calls. A senior nuance is that if you cannot cleanly separate the data and the deployment, that is often a sign the services were split along the wrong boundaries, and the right fix may be to merge them back into a modular monolith rather than press on with a distributed monolith. Another nuance is that the distributed monolith is frequently the result of prematurely splitting a system into microservices before the boundaries were understood, which is why starting as a modular monolith and extracting services only when a real need arises is the safer path.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India split its loan platform into loan, account, fraud, and credit services, but it became a distributed monolith.

Problem 1 — The shared cabinet. All four services read and wrote the same loans database. When the account service added a column, the loan and fraud services broke until all four were redeployed together. This is the shared-database symptom; the fix is database-per-service.

Problem 2 — The chained phone call. Approving a loan meant loan calls account calls fraud calls credit, all synchronous. When the credit service was slow, loan's threads blocked, its pool exhausted, and the whole approval path went down. This is the synchronous-chain symptom; the fix is async events plus circuit breakers.

Problem 3 — The shared binder. A common library held the Loan domain model with business logic. Any change meant rebuilding and redeploying all four services the same day. This is the shared-library symptom; the fix is sharing only contracts.

We will contrast the bad and good designs. The bad `CoupledLoanService` calls account, fraud, and credit synchronously in a chain and shares a database. The good `DecoupledLoanService` owns its own data, publishes an event, and uses a circuit breaker for the one synchronous call it truly needs.

The code will model a synchronous chain that cascades a failure, then a decoupled version that publishes an event and uses a timeout plus circuit breaker, showing the good version surviving a slow dependency.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
javac DistributedMonolithDemo.java
java DistributedMonolithDemo

# To avoid a distributed monolith in real systems:
#  - database-per-service (no shared tables / cross-service SQL joins)
#  - share contracts (OpenAPI/Avro) not domain libraries
#  - async events (Kafka) instead of long synchronous chains
#  - resilience4j circuit breakers + timeouts on remaining sync calls
#  - backward-compatible API versioning so deploy order does not matter
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: loan approval with downstream account and fraud healthy but credit slow/failing.

Step 1 — The coupled service approves LN-1 by calling account, then fraud, then credit, all synchronously in a chain. Account and fraud succeed, but credit is slow and fails.

Step 2 — Because the chain is synchronous, the credit failure propagates straight back and the entire LN-1 approval fails, even though the only truly broken dependency was credit. The request's fate was tied to the weakest hop — the cascade that defines a distributed monolith.

Step 3 — The decoupled service approves LN-G1 differently. It wraps the one genuinely synchronous dependency (credit) in a circuit breaker, and it pushes the non-critical account and fraud work onto an event bus instead of a synchronous chain.

Step 4 — Credit fails, but the circuit breaker catches it, returns a fallback, and the loan is still recorded. The LoanApproved event is published so fraud and account react independently and asynchronously. One slow dependency no longer blocks the request.

Step 5 — After three failures the circuit breaker opens, so further credit calls fail fast with the fallback instead of waiting and piling up blocked threads. The decoupled design survives the exact condition that took down the coupled one, which is the practical difference between a true microservice and a distributed monolith.

```
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [INFO] === distributed monolith: synchronous chain cascades ===
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [SEVERE] Loan LN-1 FAILED: chain broke at a downstream hop
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [INFO] === decoupled: event + circuit breaker survives slow dependency ===
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [WARNING] Downstream failed (1/3)
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [INFO] EVENT LoanApproved published for LN-G1 (consumers react independently)
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [INFO] Loan LN-G1 recorded (creditCheck=true, fraud/account via async events)
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [WARNING] Downstream failed (2/3)

2026-10-24 16:41:30 [WARNING] Downstream failed (3/3)
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [SEVERE] Circuit OPENED
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [INFO] Loan LN-G3 recorded (creditCheck=true, fraud/account via async events)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A distributed monolith is a system that has been split into multiple services across the network but still cannot deploy, fail, or scale independently, so it carries all the operational complexity of microservices with none of their benefits. It is the worst of both worlds, and I identify it by three symptoms. The first is a shared database, where several services read and write the same tables, so a schema change forces coordinated simultaneous redeploys and one service's heavy query starves the others. The second is shared libraries containing business logic or domain models, so changing the library forces rebuilding and redeploying every service that uses it. The third is long synchronous call chains, where one service calls another calls another within a single request, so latency is the sum of all hops, availability is the product of all their availabilities, and a single slow dependency blocks threads and cascades failure backward through the callers.

I avoid it with a set of concrete practices. I give each service its own database so it owns its data exclusively and others access it only through its API or through events, never by reaching into its tables. I share contracts, not code, meaning I publish API and event schemas and thin stubs but keep business logic inside each service, so a schema can evolve in a backward-compatible way without forcing lockstep redeploys. I favor asynchronous events over synchronous chains, so a service publishes an event and moves on instead of blocking on a chain of downstream calls. And where a synchronous call is genuinely necessary, I wrap it in timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, and fallbacks so one slow dependency cannot drag down its callers.

In my loan platform the distributed monolith showed up clearly: all four services shared one database so a column change broke them together, and loan approval was a synchronous chain through account, fraud, and credit, so when credit was slow the whole approval path collapsed. I fixed it by giving each service its own database, moving the fraud and account work onto an event bus so they react independently, and wrapping the one remaining synchronous credit check in a circuit breaker, after which a slow credit service no longer took down loan approval.

The senior judgment I always add is that if you genuinely cannot separate the data and the deployment, that is usually a sign the services were split along the wrong boundaries, and the right move may be to merge them back into a modular monolith rather than push on with a distributed monolith. This is why I prefer to start as a modular monolith and extract services only when a real need for independent deployment or scaling appears.

The one-line summary I give is: a distributed monolith is microservices that still deploy, fail, and scale together through shared databases, shared code, and synchronous chains, so you avoid it by isolating each service's data, sharing contracts rather than code, decoupling with asynchronous events, evolving APIs compatibly, and adding resilience to any remaining synchronous calls.
